clinicalPearls: SPG25 is a rare autosomal recessive, complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia mapped to chromosome 6q23-q24.1, without a confirmed causative gene.
It was delineated in a recessive kindred and is distinctive for its association with intervertebral disc herniation affecting the cervical and lumbar spine.
Onset is usually in adulthood, with progressive spastic paraparesis accompanied by prominent neck and low back pain.
A sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy has been reported in affected individuals, giving a mixed upper motor neurone and peripheral picture.
The disc disease can itself cause radicular or compressive symptoms, so imaging is needed to separate degenerative spinal pathology from the underlying HSP.
Diagnosis is clinical, supported by recessive inheritance and by excluding the recessive HSP genes that are testable (for example SPG7, SPG11, SPG15).
Care is symptomatic and multidisciplinary, addressing spasticity, neuropathic and mechanical spinal pain, and any surgically remediable disc compression.
reference.pathophysiology: SPG25 is an autosomal recessive complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia localised by linkage and homozygosity mapping to chromosome 6q23-q24.1; no gene within the interval has been confirmed, so its molecular basis is not established. The neurological phenotype reflects the HSP hallmark of a length-dependent degeneration of the corticospinal tracts, with additional dorsal column and peripheral nerve involvement accounting for the reported sensorimotor neuropathy. A striking and unusual feature is multilevel intervertebral disc herniation, suggesting that the underlying (as yet unidentified) gene product may also influence connective-tissue or intervertebral disc integrity; this dual central-nervous-system and musculoskeletal involvement is what sets SPG25 apart from the purely neuronal HSP loci.
additionalDifferentials: SPG7 (paraplegin) — common recessive complicated HSP, often with ataxia or optic atrophy
SPG11 (spatacsin) and SPG15 (spastizin/ZFYVE26) — recessive HSP with thin corpus callosum and cognitive change
Degenerative cervical or lumbar spondylotic myelopathy and radiculopathy in their own right
Hereditary motor and sensory neuropathies with pyramidal features
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the whole spine to define disc herniation and exclude cord or root compression
Genetic testing of testable recessive HSP genes (SPG7, SPG11, SPG15 and others) and exome analysis
Nerve conduction studies and EMG to characterise the peripheral neuropathy
MRI brain to look for thin corpus callosum or white matter change seen in other complicated subtypes
Very-long-chain fatty acids, vitamin B12, copper and caeruloplasmin to exclude metabolic myeloneuropathy
Assessment by spinal surgery where there is nerve root or cord compression
redFlags: New or worsening radicular pain, a sensory level or sphincter disturbance suggesting acute cord or root compression from disc herniation
Rapidly progressive weakness that outpaces the expected slow HSP course
Systemic features such as weight loss or fever pointing to an infective or neoplastic spinal lesion
Severe early sensory ataxia or areflexia suggesting a predominant neuropathy needing separate work-up
reference.prognosis: SPG25 progresses slowly, but disability can be compounded by the mechanical and radicular consequences of recurrent disc herniation. Overall life expectancy is not usually shortened, though mobility and pain control often require long-term multidisciplinary input.
pitfalls: Attributing all symptoms to degenerative disc disease and missing the underlying inherited spastic paraplegia (or the reverse)
Expecting a positive gene test — SPG25 remains a linkage-defined entity with no confirmed gene
Overlooking the peripheral neuropathy, which can be masked by upper motor neurone signs
Proceeding to spinal surgery expecting it to resolve the spasticity, which arises centrally rather than from the disc disease
references: Hereditary spastic paraplegia clinical genetics reviews
Neurogenetics reference databases (gene and locus catalogues)
management: No disease-specific therapy exists; manage lower-limb spasticity with oral antispasticity agents such as baclofen or tizanidine and focal botulinum toxin
Multimodal management of the neck and low-back pain from multilevel intervertebral disc herniation, with analgesia, physiotherapy and pain-service input
Spinal surgical assessment where disc herniation causes nerve-root or cord compression
Podiatry and orthotic management of the associated sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy
Physiotherapy, stretching and walking aids to preserve gait and prevent contractures
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance with cascade testing of relatives
Escalate for surgical decompression or urgent neurological review if compressive symptoms worsen
